objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
This is a fair question about a genuinely difficult word, and it deserves a careful answer rather than a dismissal.

The key move is to let Paul interpret his own term. If "firstborn of all creation" meant "first created thing," Colossians 1:16 would immediately contradict it: "for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible... all things were created by him, and for him." A creature cannot be the one "by whom" and "for whom" all creatures exist — that would make Christ both included in "all things" and the maker of "all things," which is incoherent. The most natural reading is that prototokos here functions as a title of rank and priority, not birth sequence — exactly the sense it carries in Psalm 89:27, where God calls David "my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth," even though David was neither God's literal child nor first in any chronological sense. In both Hellenistic and biblical usage, "firstborn" regularly designates preeminence and inheritance-right, the position of supremacy over an estate — which is precisely what Colossians 1 is building toward: Christ as heir of all things and head over all.

This isn't importing later theology into the text; it's reading Paul's sentence as a whole rather than isolating one clause. John 1:3 says exactly the same thing with maximal generality — "all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" — which leaves no room for Christ to be one of the "made" things. So the line runs through all reality between Creator and creature, and Colossians 1:15–17 places Christ, "firstborn" and all, on the Creator's side of that line.

# Objection: "Firstborn" clearly means created

Look, Colossians 1:15 calls Jesus the *firstborn of all creation*—*prototokos tēs ktiseōs*. In ordinary Greek and Hebrew usage, "firstborn" (*bĕkôr*, *prototokos*) means the first-born *child*, the one who came into being first. If Paul wanted to say Jesus was eternally divine and not created, why would he use language that—in every other biblical context—describes creatures? The parallelism is unavoidable: he is firstborn *of* creation, meaning *part of* the created order, the first and highest creature. How do you get around the plain meaning of the word without importing later theological categories into the text?
